analysis.one_liner: Creates personal Social Security investment accounts alongside a guaranteed federal benefit and raises survivor benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in December 2001 with 6 Republican cosponsors, never got a committee markup or floor vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any worker 18 or older elect to have the Treasury deposit a yearly credit — about 3% of wages up to the payroll-tax cap, plus 2% above it — into a personal investment account, funded from the general Treasury rather than the payroll tax. The account, invested 60% in broad stock indexes and 40% in high-grade corporate bonds through a certified account manager, would pay a monthly supplement on top of a legally guaranteed Social Security benefit. It also raised widow's and widower's benefits, credited years spent caring for children, repealed the earnings test at 62, and cut the government pension offset from two-thirds to one-third.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who elect the accounts, who would build personal savings on top of a guaranteed benefit; widows, widowers, and disabled survivors, who would get higher minimum benefits; caregivers, whose child-care years would count more toward benefits; government pensioners, whose offset would shrink; and certified investment managers, who would hold the accounts for a fee.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electing workers, widows, caregivers, and investment managers

how_it_helps.text: Any individual age 18 or older could elect to become a covered individual and receive annual refundable credits — 3% of wages up to a cap plus 2% above it — deposited into a personal Social Security guarantee account funded from the Treasury general fund [S2][S3].

Account assets would be invested 60% in portfolios tracking broad common stock indexes and 40% in diversified high-grade corporate bonds, held by a certified account manager subject to fiduciary rules [S3].

The Secretary of the Treasury would issue each beneficiary a certificate representing a legally enforceable guarantee of full Social Security benefits with accurate annual cost-of-living adjustments [S2].

Retirees would receive a 5% lump sum from their account at benefit entitlement, and a monthly 'account distribution supplement' on top of their regular benefit; at death, remaining account assets would go to the decedent's estate free of estate tax [S3].

The bill raises widow's and widower's benefits to a minimum, extends benefits to disabled widows and widowers regardless of age, repeals the seven-year disability restriction, waives the two-year divorcee waiting period when the ex-spouse remarries, credits more earnings for caregivers, and cuts the government pension offset from two-thirds to one-third of the pension [S2].
The earnings test — which cuts benefits for beneficiaries 62 and older who keep working — would be repealed for those over 62, letting early retirees work without losing benefits [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, because the account credits come out of the Treasury general fund rather than the payroll tax; account holders also bear market risk on the account portion, pay administrative fees of up to 0.25% a year, and would owe income tax on the supplements as Social Security benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and account holders' returns

drawbacks.text: The account credits would be paid 'from amounts otherwise available in the general fund of the Treasury,' not from payroll taxes — meaning the added cost of the new accounts would fall on all federal taxpayers rather than on the Social Security trust funds, a multi-trillion-dollar commitment over decades under the plans of this era [S3].

Account balances rise and fall with 'earnings credited' and 'losses' from investment, so the monthly annuity and supplement would depend on market performance, even though the underlying Part A benefit would be guaranteed [S3].
Account assets are available to pay the program's administrative costs, including account managers' fees, capped at 25 basis points a year — a recurring drag on workers' account balances [S3].

Supplements paid from the accounts would be taxable as Social Security benefits, and the estate-tax exemption for account assets would let balances pass to heirs outside the estate tax, a benefit skewed toward heirs of larger accounts [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs real benefit improvements for widows, caregivers, and early retirees with a sweeping restructuring that adds a large, permanent call on the general Treasury to finance personal accounts. The guaranteed benefit floor and enforceable certificate protect the basic promise, but the account portion carries market risk, fees, and a cost shift from the payroll tax to general revenue that the bill itself requires an annual report to track [S3]. It was a serious, fully drafted proposal, but its fiscal scale was the core of the debate it never got to have.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, sat there through the sponsor's remarks the next day, and never received a markup or floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. E. Clay Shaw Jr. (R-FL) introduced the Social Security Guarantee Plus Act on December 13, 2001, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
Six House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
Shaw delivered introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on December 14, 2001 [S5].
The action history shows no further activity: no subcommittee or full committee markup, no vote, and no discharge petition before the Congress ended January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's passage because it never advanced: workers got no accounts and no benefit increases, and investment managers got no new accounts. What was preserved was the existing Social Security structure, unchanged, with no new general-fund commitment.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing system; no accounts were created

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were House Republicans, with none of the chamber's 208 Democrats signing on; the bill was a Republican-authored Social Security personal-accounts proposal in the wake of President Bush's 2001 Social Security commission.

industries.note: The bill would make qualified asset managers the permanent, mandatory channel for workers' retirement savings as board-certified 'account managers,' with fees of up to 0.25% a year deducted from account assets. The required 60% broad stock index and 40% high-grade corporate bond allocation would guarantee the industry a vast new pool of payroll-derived money to manage for a fee.
Mandating that 40% of every account be held in diversified high-grade corporate bonds would create a large, steady new source of demand for corporate debt, lowering borrowing costs for bond issuers.
